raw_response:
## Best fit: BlockTube

I would start with [BlockTube](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube). It is designed to filter particular YouTube channels and videos, including channel-ID rules, rather than trying to block YouTube at the network level. Its documentation says playlists and autoplay can continue while unwanted content is filtered. A stable channel ID is the most precise starting point for each ARTE channel you want to exclude.

The practical setup is to add the unwanted uploader through BlockTube's channel-blocking menu, then repeat for any other ARTE channels that appear. Its [dated context-menu instructions](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube/wiki/Context-Menus) explain the channel-blocking action. A reupload by another uploader will require its own channel or title rule; blocking a broadcaster's official channel cannot identify every copy of its documentaries.

The [options source](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube/blob/master/src/ui/options.html) contains both a control for advancing after a block and a control that limits blocking to suggestions. For your unattended-listening use case, review those settings and verify that a blocked video cannot start through the route you normally use. This is a documentation-based recommendation, not a claim that I installed or tested the extension. The [Firefox listing](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/blocktube/) identifies version 0.4.8 dated February 7, 2026, before the June 9, 2026 cutoff; the inspected live source is not a historical snapshot.

## Other candidates, ranked

**2. [Channel Blocker](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/channel-blocker/nfkmalbckemmklibjddenhnofgnfcdfp).** This offers channel/user blacklisting and regular-expression filtering, so it is another practical candidate for removing ARTE-related videos. The official listing dates version 3.0.5 to August 4, 2024 and links its [public repository](https://github.com/Time-Machine-Development/Channel-Blocker-Manifest-v3). The important unresolved point is autoplay: the inspected listing establishes filtering but does not establish that a hidden recommendation cannot still begin playing. I would check that behavior before using it as protection while dozing.

**3. [YouTube's own Autoplay switch](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6327615?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop&hl=en).** If the main objective is to stop an unwanted next video from waking you, turn this off on the device you use. YouTube's help explains that the setting controls automatic playback of another related video after the current one ends. This is a direct alternative mechanism, although it also stops automatic continuation into desirable documentaries and does not hide ARTE in search or recommendations. Do not assume the cited explanation covers every playlist mode. The live help article is undated, so its date status is unknown.

**4. [Language & Keyword Filter for YouTube](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/yt-language-and-keyword-filter/).** This Firefox add-on can filter keywords in video titles, channel names and playlist titles, including content loaded as you browse. A rule matching ARTE could catch branded uploads across more than one uploader, but it can also miss unlabelled copies or match unrelated text. Its description does not establish prevention of autoplay, so I rank it below the channel-focused option and the playback switch for this particular problem. The inspected version, 1.0.3.2 dated October 3, 2026, is later evidence; I have not verified what an earlier version could do.

For the channel-specific requirement, BlockTube is the strongest documented fit among these findings. For stopping surprise playback altogether, the built-in autoplay setting is the simpler fallback. None of these findings establishes that all ARTE-produced material can be recognized regardless of uploader, title or browser changes.

Research limits: public GitHub repository and code-search attempts were blocked. Public source was instead discovered through a web-indexed GitHub code search and inspected on its public page; this was code-through-web, not successful native code search. No excluded question thread or its answers were opened, and no runtime installation or account access was used.
